nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the Whig criticism of the Edinburgh Review and the Scottish legal and literary culture of the early nineteenth century
literary_identity: Advocate, critic and judge; the founder and long editor of the Edinburgh Review, the maker of the modern review article as an instrument of literary and political power, and the most feared English-language critic of the Romantic generation.
biography: Jeffrey was born in Charles Street in Edinburgh on 23 October 1773, the son of a depute-keeper of the signet, and was educated at the Royal High School and at the University of Edinburgh, from which he was withdrawn at fourteen and sent to complete his studies at home in the classics. He studied law, was admitted to the Scottish bar in 1794, and passed the 1790s in a literary Edinburgh society in which the terrors of the French Revolution and the trials of the Scottish radicals had made liberal opinion cautious. With Sydney Smith, Horner and Brougham he projected a quarterly journal, and the Edinburgh Review began in October 1802 with his article on the peerage, which he wrote at once as a defence of the new undertaking and as a statement of its principles. He edited the journal to 1829, wrote the critical and review articles in enormous number, and practised at the English bar after 1815, taking silk in 1821. His reputation for severe and elegant judgement made him the arbiter of Romantic poetry: his treatment of Wordsworth, of Byron and of the Lake school established the review as a power in letters, and his name gave the enterprise the credibility that a Scotch and Whig quarterly needed in a loyal and Tory reading public. In 1830 he went to the bench as a lord of session and justiciary under the title Lord Jeffrey, from which office his death at London on 26 January 1850 relieved a career that had long been more legal than critical. His contributions to the later numbers of the Review were collected and reprinted, and his correspondence and the memoirs of his brother-in-law Lord Cockburn remain the chief record of the circle that founded the journal.
literary_profile: His literary form is the review article, and he practised it as a genre of its own: a discursive essay that reviews books as occasions for argument on constitution, finance, education, religion and taste, written in the first person plural of the journal and closing with an assessment of a nation's condition. His critical papers on the poets and novelists of the day, on the Scottish law schools and on the Whig historians, and his contributions on the French revolutionary and post-revolutionary writers, make up a continuous commentary on the literature of the first third of the century; his editorial and political articles on the peerage, on Catholic emancipation and on reform are documents of Whig argument.
stylistic_characteristics: A polished, urban and deliberately moderate irony, in which severity of judgement is carried in the language of good-breeding; long circumstantial periods, understatement, the concession that precedes the demolition, and a marked use of the collective editorial voice. The prose is rhetorical rather than technical, and its effects depend on balance, on the well-placed aside, and on a self-conscious elegance which his opponents read as the arrogance of the critic.
intellectual_concerns: The authority of criticism and its relation to party and to patronage; the freedom of the press and of review against the quarterlies and the publishers; the Whig account of liberty, of the peerage and of reform; the taste and the standing of the new Romantic poetry, and the charge of egotism and of deliberate vulgarity brought against it; the place of Scottish letters within a British public; the relation of religion, education and political temper in a commercial society.
historical_significance: He made the Edinburgh Review the model of the literary-quarterly as a political institution and gave the review article its modern authority and its modern weapon, and for a generation English Romantic writing was read, priced and judged in relation to his verdicts. His editorship established the practice of the unsigned but personally identified critic, and his career from bar to bench is the central case of the union of letters and public office in nineteenth-century Britain. He also fixed the shape of the anti-Romantic reception, since the famous quarrel over the Lake poets began with his pages.
biographical_uncertainty: The attribution of individual unsigned articles in the early numbers of the Edinburgh Review is still in part a matter of inference from diary, correspondence and the ledgers of the journal, and the standard tables of attribution are not unanimous. His birth is given in some earlier biographical accounts at the family place of Argaty near Doune in Perthshire rather than in Edinburgh, though the Edinburgh parochial and school records support the city.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English (Cornish); the Regency science and literary culture of Bristol and the metropolitan institution
literary_identity: Chemist, lecturer and poet; the most brilliant public expositor of the new chemistry, the founder of electro-chemical investigation in Britain, and a representative figure of the union of science, literature and celebrity in the Romantic period.
biography: Davy was born at Penzance in Cornwall on 17 December 1778, the second of eight children of a carpenter and portrait-painter of modest means, and was put out as an apprentice to his brother John, a Penzance surgeon, where the pharmacy and a chance of chemistry first attracted him. Removed to Bristol in 1798 by Thomas Beddoes, he worked at the Pneumatic Institution founded for the trial of the new gases in disease, and the experiments on nitrous oxide and on other aeriform fluids recorded in the Researches, Chemical and Philosophical of 1800 made his name. He came to London as assistant lecturer at the metropolitan institution and from 1802 delivered the annual course that made him the most attended scientific speaker in the kingdom, lecturing on agriculture, on the chemistry of combustion and respiration, and, before a mixed fashionable audience, on the powers of the new science. In 1807 and 1808, with the great battery of the institution, he decomposed the fixed alkalis and the earths and isolated the metals of potash and soda, and he established the electro-chemical doctrine of affinity; he was knighted in 1812, and the Elements of Chemical Philosophy of that year, the first part only of a projected treatise, gathered the new chemistry into a philosophy. Returned to Parliament for the Devon borough of Ashburton in 1812, he also took the professional care of mining safety that produced the safety lamp of 1815, the instrument for which he refused a patent. He was president of the Royal Society from 1820 until ill health compelled his resignation in 1827; his marriage of 1812 had ended in separation, and after leaving the presidency he set out on a last tour of the Continent, dying at Geneva on 29 May 1829 at the age of fifty, a figure of celebrity whom the literary public remembered as a poet and a moralist of science as well as a chemist.
literary_profile: His scientific writing is at once an experimental record and a public performance: the Bristol volume of 1800 is a narrative of inquiry, with the history of the compound, the account of the inhalations made on his own body and on his friends, and the physiological speculation about respiration and animal heat, while the Elements of Chemical Philosophy of 1812 states the doctrines of the elements, of the atomic theory and of electro-chemical affinity as a complete system, and closes with a celebrated prospectus of the power of chemical discovery. He left also lectures on agricultural chemistry, papers to the Royal Society, a set of early poems and dramatic attempts preserved in his notebooks, and a large correspondence.
stylistic_characteristics: A lecture prose of great rhetorical command, in which the experimental narrative is arranged as discovery, with the sentence of wonder, the apostrophe to nature and the elevated close on the uses of science; the technical writing is clear, generalising and ambitious of system, and it self-consciously claims the imagination for the chemist. His early verse and the manuscripts of his youth show an accomplished Romantic diction of the school he read, and the two manner, the poetical and the philosophical, are continuous in the public lectures.
intellectual_concerns: The chemical constitution of bodies and the electrical origin of affinity; the decomposition of the earths and alkalis and the nature of the elements; the chemistry of respiration, of animal heat and of the effects of gases upon living bodies; the safety of the miner and the duty of the scientist to useful invention; the relation of physical enquiry to poetry, to religion and to public improvement; the limits of the atomic and the electro-chemical explanations.
historical_significance: He founded electro-chemistry as a branch of the science, established the list of the elements as it stood before the periodic scheme, and gave the Royal Institution its public character, making the scientific lecture a fashionable and literary event for the first time in England. His safety lamp, adopted with modifications after the inquiry into coal mining, was the first great instrument of industrial humanity produced by scientific method, and his presidency of the Royal Society and his teaching of Michael Faraday place him at the origin of the professional scientific culture of Victorian Britain.
biographical_uncertainty: The chronology of his Cornish apprenticeship and of the removal to Bristol is given with small variations in the biographies, and the dating of his earliest verse and dramatic manuscripts is uncertain. The full extent of his authorship of anonymous reviews and of contributions to the fashionable literary and scientific journals of the 1800s has never been settled, and the records of the inhalation experiments at Bristol survive only as he and Beddoes reported them.

alternative_names: The author of the History of British India
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the philosophical radical and Utilitarian school, and the political economy of the Ricardian writers
literary_identity: Historian, economist and logician of the Utilitarian school; the writer who gave British rule in India its most influential English history, who first made Ricardian political economy teachable, and whose plan of education and whose controversial reviews shaped the radical thought of a generation.
biography: Mill was born at Northwater Bridge in the parish of Logie Pert in Forfarshire on 6 April 1773, the son of a cobbler who held a small piece of land, and was named James Milne, the spelling of the family name being altered later in life. He was taught at the parish school and at the Montrose burgh school, took the M.A. at King's College Aberdeen in 1798, and was licensed by a Secession presbytery, serving for a time as a dissenting chaplain and schoolmaster before private tuition in Fife gave him leisure for scholarship. He came to London in 1810 with the intention of emigrating to America, and stayed, writing for the Encyclopaedia Britannica and the Critical Review and editing a short-lived journal. Through Joseph Hume he met Jeremy Bentham in 1808-1810 and became his disciple, friend and for a decade his most devoted public advocate. The three volumes of the History of British India, published in 1817 and written entirely from books, made his reputation and an opening in official opinion; he entered East India House as an examiner in 1823 and rose to be chief of the office, and from that position, and later through his son's influence, he acted on the appointments and educational policy of the company's service. The Elements of Political Economy of 1821 stated the Ricardian doctrine in the form of a textbook, and his contributions to the Edinburgh and Westminster Reviews made him the most feared controversialist of the philosophical radicals. He helped found the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge and University College London, and he educated his son John Stuart Mill under a documented and much-criticised plan of instruction. He died in London on 23 June 1836, having long been a figure of official influence and of party suspicion.
literary_profile: His literary work is argumentative and systematic rather than imaginative: a three-volume history that treats the civilisations of India as stages of improvement to be judged by European standards of science and law; a compact economic textbook built on a few rigorous definitions and on the doctrine that demand does not regulate production; and a vast body of review essay, pamphlet and encyclopaedia article on government, jurisprudence, colonies, education and the analysis of the human mind. His Fragment on Finance and his articles on the Law of Nations and on Colonies carry the same school of argument into the general literature of the period, and his Analysis of the Phenomena of the Human Mind, published posthumously with his son's notes, closes the associationist tradition of Hartley and Locke.
stylistic_characteristics: A dry, lucid and unrelenting prose of definition, division and deduction, in which a proposition is isolated, supported by enumeration and then applied without concession to feeling or authority; long sentences of parallel members, abstract terms handled as instruments, and a polemic that is severe rather than witty. In the history the manner becomes judicial and rhetorical, with the repeated verdict of stationary, despotic and childish upon whole civilisations.
intellectual_concerns: The application of the associationist psychology of Locke and Hartley to the whole of mind and society; the principle of utility as the measure of institutions, of punishment and of education; the government of India, its history and its reform; the laws of value, wages, profit and rent, and the division of wealth; the representative and educative function of a democratic institution; the relation of religion to priestcraft and to state; the proper ends and methods of instruction.
historical_significance: The History of British India was for a century the standard English account of the subcontinent and a decisive influence on the policy and the self-justification of the company's rule, as well as the textbook against which later Indian historians wrote. The Elements of Political Economy made Ricardian doctrine transmissible, and his official position at East India House gave Utilitarian principle an unusual direct effect on appointments, education and administration. As Bentham's chief public advocate and as the father and first teacher of John Stuart Mill he stands at the centre of the philosophical radicalism that links the Utilitarian school to Victorian thought.
biographical_uncertainty: The family name was Milne, and Mill wrote of his own boyhood in the autobiographical material later used by his son, whose account is the principal source for the years before 1810 and is necessarily retrospective. The exact chronology of his chaplaincies, schoolmastering and tutoring in Scotland in the years 1798-1810 is variously set down in the biographies.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish-born English; the dissenting hymnody and the reform journalism of the northern manufacturing towns
literary_identity: Hymn-writer, poet and editor of a manufacturing-town newspaper; the most widely sung of the evangelical hymnists of his generation and a combative Whig and abolitionist journalist.
biography: Montgomery was born at Irvine in Ayrshire on 4 November 1771, the second of the four children of a Moravian itinerant preacher of poor means, and at about six years of age was sent to board at the Moravian school and community at Fulneck near Leeds, where he was educated and from which, on the death of his parents in the West Indies, he was bound apprentice in 1787 to a Sheffield printer. His master Joseph Goforth, proprietor of the Sheffield Register, fled to America in 1792 to avoid prosecution, and the nineteen-year-old apprentice carried on the paper as the Sheffield Register and Independent Miscellany, and after a change of title and of politics established it in 1794 as the Sheffield Iris, of which he was proprietor and editor until 1825. He was imprisoned in 1795 for nine months for a seditious article on the arbitrary measures of the government, and again in 1810 for reporting in full a speech delivered at a public meeting in his town, and both commitments made him a recognised figure in the controversy about the liberty of the press. He removed from the Moravian to the Unitarian connection, preached and taught, and supported Catholic relief, the abolition of slavery, education for the labouring poor and factory reform, using the Iris as a register of the manufacturing district's agitations as well as a vehicle for his own verse. In 1825 he retired to London to conduct the Christian Observer, the evangelical monthly founded by the supporters of the Church Missionary Society, and he edited it until his death, publishing in the same years a volume of hymns and several longer poems, of which The World before the Flood and the songs and ballads of the Iris were the best known. He died at the Mount, near Sheffield, on 30 April 1854, and was buried in the General Cemetery there, having become the most frequently sung of the hymn-writers of his connection.
literary_profile: His work is divided between the hymn, the occasional and narrative poem and the newspaper. The hymns, written mostly for congregational singing and for the anniversaries of the evangelical connection, are compressed, strictly metrical and deliberately simple, and a large number of them passed into the standard hymnals. The verse of the Iris years includes songs, ballads and topographical and political lyrics, and the later volumes carry scriptural and oriental subjects treated in the long manner; his journalism, editorial, reported and correspondence, is the bulk of his printed remains, together with the speeches and tracts of the reform and missionary causes he served.
stylistic_characteristics: A clear, tuneful and strictly metrical verse manner, built on short lines, on balanced stanzas and on the strong close of the hymn; an ear for the singable phrase, and a marked preference for concrete image over abstraction. The journalistic prose is brisk, indignant and personal, with the report, the editorial stroke and the appeal to the readership of a manufacturing town all fused in a single number.
intellectual_concerns: The duties and liberties of the press in a time of war and of domestic alarm; the service of the evangelical and dissenting communities by their own verse and their own news; the sin of the slave trade and of colonial oppression, and the obligations of the emancipation cause; the education of the labouring poor and the Sabbath and Sunday-school; the providential reading of public history and of national judgment.
historical_significance: He gave the English hymnody of the nineteenth century some of its most permanently sung tunes and texts, and his example helped to make the denominational hymn a recognised literary form; as editor of the Iris he created the model of the independent manufacturing-town newspaper, and his imprisonments were cited for a generation in the argument for the freedom of reporting. He is one of the clearest instances of the union of evangelical dissent, reform journalism and abolitionist publicity in the northern industrial counties.
biographical_uncertainty: The details of his apprenticeship and of the transfer of the Sheffield Register to his hands in 1792 are recorded chiefly from his own prefaces and from the memoirs written after his death, and the two accounts differ on the dating of the first number under his management. The authorship of unsigned editorial matter in the Register and the Iris is not recoverable, and the list of his contributions to other journals has never been settled. His parents' year and place of death in the West Indies, and the length and the prison of his first commitment, are variously stated in the biographies.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Anglo-Irish; the Irish tale and the fiction of national character, and the educational writing of the Edgeworthstown household
literary_identity: Novelist of Anglo-Irish society and writer for children; the founder of the Irish national tale and of the realist provincial novel in English, and with her father the author of the period's great treatise of educational practice.
biography: Edgeworth was born at Black Bourton in Oxfordshire, the estate of her mother's family, on 1 January 1768, the eldest daughter and third child of Richard Lovell Edgeworth and of Honora Sneyd, his second wife, and she was brought up in the large household of Edgeworthstown in the county of Longford, where her father's scheme of practical education was tried upon his children and where she learned languages, science, pottery-work and the management of an estate. Her mother died in 1776 and her father married her sister Elizabeth, and the education of the household continued unchanged; from her teens she wrote tales, translations and plays for the family theatre and for the instruction of the younger children. She began to publish to increase the income of a property embarrassed by her father's speculations and by his fourth marriage, and the two volumes of Practical Education, written with him and issued in 1798, were the first substantial work of her household to reach the public. Castle Rackrent, printed anonymously in 1800, gave the English novel its first Irish family history told by the steward of three successive masters, and the Irish tales of the Popular Tales of 1804 extended the same analysis of the tenantry, the absentee and the ascendancy; Ennui, The Absentee of 1812 and Patronage of 1814 made her the most read novelist of the Irish question, and the Tales of a Grandfather, begun in 1810, supplied the standard English history written for young readers. She moved in the literary and political society of London and Paris, was visited and corresponded with by the chief writers of the day, and observed with a close and anxious eye the operation of the union, of the Catholic question and of distress in her own county. She edited and printed her father's Memoirs in 1820 and 1821, continued to publish tales and juvenile books through the 1820s, never married, and after her father's death governed the household and the estate. She died at Edgeworthstown on 22 May 1849, the first Irish novelist of consequence in English and one of the most quoted writers on education and on national character.
literary_profile: Her work divides between the Irish tale of national and provincial character, the novel of opinion and of the educated family, the history and story written for children and young readers, and the educational, political and personal letters. Castle Rackrent introduced the framing of an Irish narrative by an oral servant voice and the comic use of a family history to expose a class, and the Popular Tales, Ennui, The Absentee and Patronage carry the same analysis of Anglo-Irish society into other forms. Practical Education, written with her father, reports the experiments of a cultivated household and argues from the principles of the philosophy of the mind to the practice of the nursery, and her tales for young readers, with the later family and literary correspondence, make a substantial prose work of instruction and of observation.
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, rapid and conversational prose of dialogue, of circumstance and of the telling small fact, with the didactic manner always in view of the reader's pleasure; in the Irish tales the voice is deliberately oral, digressive, full of the proverb, the aside and the understatement of the servant-narrator, and the irony is carried by the speaker's own innocence. The educational and letters writing is exact, dry and unpretentious, and the tales for children give the same concrete method to the instruction of the young.
intellectual_concerns: The character and the government of Ireland, the absentee system, the tenantry and the politics of the union; the education of the infant and child mind, the association of ideas and the discipline of the natural consequence; the morals of opinion, of patronage and of the man of science in a family and a county; the condition and the employment of women and of the governess; the making of national history for the young, and the ethics of how a conquest is remembered.
historical_significance: She founded the Irish national tale and the realist novel of provincial and national character in English, and the framing and the oral irony of Castle Rackrent made it the starting point of the modern Irish novel and a model for the historical fiction of the following generation. Practical Education carried associationist psychology into nursery and schoolroom practice and set the terms of the family literature of instruction, and her tales and histories for children were standard reading in English-speaking schoolrooms for a century; as an observer of the Irish ascendancy she is also a primary witness of the society that the union changed.
biographical_uncertainty: The division of labour between father and daughter in Practical Education, and in the household experiments which that book reports, is not wholly separable, and the account of her education and of the family theatrics rests largely on her own recollections and on the Memoirs of her father which she edited. The dating of her early unpublished tales and translations, and the extent of her share in the joint educational volumes issued under her father's name and hers, are variously stated in the biographies.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Whig historical and essayistic prose of the mid-nineteenth century
literary_identity: Essayist, narrative historian, poet of the ballad revival and Whig parliamentarian; the most widely read English prose stylist of his generation and the representative voice of liberal historical optimism.
biography: Macaulay was born at Rothley Temple in Leicestershire on 25 October 1800, the eldest son of Zachary Macaulay, the Scottish evangelist and abolitionist who had been governor of Sierra Leone, and of Selina Mills, the daughter of a Quaker banker; the family's abolitionist and Clapham connections shaped his earliest convictions. A precocious reader, he wrote an epic-poem plan as a schoolboy at the Hill House school in Huntingdon and won prizes at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he joined the Cambridge discussers and won the Chancellors medal for an English essay on Milton. Called to the bar in 1826, he abandoned practice for letters and politics, and his essay on Milton in the Edinburgh Review in 1825 began a career of review-writing that made him the acknowledged master of the Whig essay. Elected to Parliament for Cambridge in 1830, he served in the Grey ministry as Paymaster of the Forces, took a leading part in the reform bill debates, and went to India in 1834 as a member of the governors council, where his Minute on Education of 1835 argued for English-language instruction and had lasting consequences for Indian policy. He returned to England in 1838, declined office for a decade, and published in 1842 the Lays of Ancient Rome, his most popular verse. The first two volumes of the History of England from the Accession of James the Second appeared in 1848 to extraordinary success, and he held office again as Secretary at War and then as Foreign Secretary in the Crimea ministry before failing to return to Parliament in 1856 and accepting a peerage as Baron Macaulay of Rothley. He died in London on 28 December 1859 and was buried in Westminster Abbey, leaving the History unfinished at the peace of Ryswick and a great body of posthumous essays, letters and diary.
literary_profile: His work is chiefly the review essay and the narrative history: the essays on English statesmen, poets and historians, collected from the Edinburgh and Foreign Reviews, which made a public philosophy of Whig progress, and the History of England, a continuous narrative of the reigns of James the Second and William the Third built out of parliamentary, memoir and newspaper sources. The Lays of Ancient Rome are ballad-like narrative poems rendered out of Roman history and designed to imitate the popular strain of ancient song, and his occasional verse, translations and schoolboy romances belong to the same accomplished literary game. The posthumous Critical and Historical Works, edited with the famous Life and Letters by his younger sister, gathered the essays, stories, and speeches that had appeared separately.
stylistic_characteristics: The most imitated English prose style of the mid-century: a rhetoric of parallelism, tricolon and balanced clauses, of emphatic negatives and self-answerings, of the abrupt short sentence after a long period, and of a confident enumeration of instances. The narrative movement is rapid and visual, the judgement always pronounced, the irony directed at opponents rather than at his own side, and the effect is oratorical, the essay being written as if from a parliamentary bench.
intellectual_concerns: The Whig account of the revolution settlement of 1688 as the source of modern liberty; the growth of wealth, of population and of letters under constitutional government; the relation of religious persecution to political power; the uses of literature as national instruction, and of English in the government of India; the character and limits of party; the place of great men and of measures in history; the confidence in improvement and its subsequent interrogation.
historical_significance: The History of England fixed for generations the popular English narrative of the seventeenth century and became one of the best-selling works of non-fiction of the century; his essays set the standard of the review article as a vehicle of political and literary argument, and the Lays supplied a schoolroom canon of narrative verse. As an educational legislator in India and as a parliamentarian of reform he influenced policy directly, and his confident Protestant Whiggery has been the chief target of the later revisionist histories it provoked.
biographical_uncertainty: His Indian minutes and despatches are numerous and were published posthumously in edited form, and the extent of his responsibility for anonymous review and magazine matter before 1830 is not wholly settled. The account of his schoolboy writings and of the Cambridge years depends largely on family memoir and on his own recollections, and the editors of the Letters and Life made deliberate omissions.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the Church of Scotland and Scottish moral philosophy, political economy and natural theology of the early nineteenth century
literary_identity: Presbyterian preacher, evangelist, political economist and professor of moral philosophy and then of theology; the most powerful Scottish religious orator of his generation and the leader of the party that formed the Free Church of Scotland in 1843.
biography: Chalmers was born at Anstruther in Fife on 17 March 1780, the sixth of the fourteen children of a shipowner and general merchant, and was put to the parish school before entering the University of St Andrews at about twelve years of age. He graduated M.A. in 1797, was licensed to preach by the clergymen of the neighbouring parishes, and served as a colleague minister at Anstruther and then at Kelvin near Glasgow, where his mathematical and astronomical abilities were already known. The years 1811-12 brought a conversion from the easy deism of his early reading to an evangelical Trinitarianism, and in 1815 he was translated to the large Trinity Church parish in Glasgow, where he threw himself into the religious and social government of a manufacturing population. There he carried out the district scheme of visiting, schooling, savings banks and poor-law administration that he reported in the discourses on the Christian and civic economy of large towns, and there also he argued, in the controversy over slavery, for immediate improvement rather than for the measures the abolitionist societies demanded, a position later used against him. He became professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow in 1823, published the first Bridgewater Treatise on the design of the inanimate world, and in the same year moved to St John's, West Edinburgh, where his preaching drew audiences far beyond the congregation. He was translated to the chair of theology at Edinburgh in 1828, took a leading part in the Ten Years' Conflict over spiritual independence and patronage, and after the Disruption of 1843 was the first moderator of the Free Church of Scotland, dying at Edinburgh on 31 May 1847 while still organising colleges, churches and missions for the new body.
literary_profile: His works divide between the sermon and the discourse, the argumentative treatise and the piece of applied social enquiry. The Bridgewater Treatise of 1823 restates the design argument from the inorganic creation for an age of expanding physical science, and the discourses on the Christian and civic economy of large towns of 1821 apply the same method to the city, arguing that a church without territorial organisation cannot govern or relieve a population that has no local ties. He wrote also astronomical and mathematical papers, articles on political economy and on the colonies for the Encyclopaedia Britannica and the Edinburgh Encyclopaedia, in which he handled the Malthusian and Ricardoian doctrines as a moralist, and a great body of popular religious and missionary tracts, sermons and letters.
stylistic_characteristics: A spoken and periodic style of great command, in which the argument is built up in balanced clauses, in the cumulative arrangement of instances and in an appeal to the imagination of the reader; the printed sermon retains the rhetorical accent, the direct address and the long swell of the pulpit. In the economic and theological treatises the manner becomes cooler, more definitional and more scholastic, and in the tracts it is homely, concrete and full of named cases from the district.
intellectual_concerns: The evidence of design in the inanimate creation and its relation to the advances of physical science; the moral government of great towns, the failure of centralised administration, and the district as the unit of church, school and relief; the adequacy of the voluntary and established systems for a manufacturing population; the duties of the state toward religion and education; the relation of political economy to morality and to Christian obligation; the claims of foreign missions and of colonial Protestantism.
historical_significance: He gave the natural-theology tradition of Paley its most ambitious nineteenth-century statement and made the Bridgewater series a landmark of the argument from design in a scientific age, and his district experiment in Glasgow supplied the model on which later Scottish and English territorial church and school administration was rebuilt. His writings on political economy carried the Malthusian and Ricardian debates into moral and religious argument for a wide audience, and his leadership of the Disruption made him the central figure of Victorian Scottish religious history.
biographical_uncertainty: His birthplace is given as Anstruther in most modern accounts and as Couper (Cowper) in some earlier biographies and archival calendars, the family having connections in both Fife towns; the day of his death is given as 30 or 31 May 1847. The extent of his responsibility for the anonymous and joint contributions in the Glasgow religious tract movement of his ministry is not fully established.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; political economy and the prose of argument of the Romantic period
literary_identity: Clerman, mathematical political economist and the first professor of a modern political economy chair in England; the writer who fixed the population argument and its relation to famine, preventive checks and the Poor Laws.
biography: Malthus was born at the Rookery, the family estate near Dorking in Surrey, on 13 or 14 February 1766, the second son of Daniel Malthus, a cultivated landowner and friend of David Hume and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and of Henrietta Graham. He was taught largely at home by tutors and by his father, then studied at Jesus College, Cambridge, where he took prizes in Latin and Greek and became a fellow in 1789. Ordained in the Church of England in 1791, he married in 1804 against the terms of his fellowship and lost it, but was in 1805 appointed professor of history and political economy at the East India Company's college at Haileybury, the first such professorship in England. His Essay on the Principle of Population, first issued anonymously in 1798 as a reply to his father's acquaintance the Marquis de Condorcet and to William Godwin's expectation of indefinite improvement, was enlarged in a second edition of 1803 into a documented historical and statistical work, with the added argument that vice and misery were the necessary consequences of population exceeding food. He became a central figure of London political economy, a friend and antagonist of David Ricardo, a frequent contributor to the debates on the Corn Laws and the Poor Laws, and from 1819 a member of the Political Economy Club and of the royal and statistical societies. His Definition of Political Economy (1827), his Measures of Value (1829) and his mathematical statements of rent were widely read and contested. He died unexpectedly at Bath on 29 December 1834 while on a visit, and was buried in the parish church at Bath, with a monument later placed in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: His writing is argumentative prose of the highest order of its kind: an anonymous pamphlet of 1798 that grew by repeated and heavily rewritten editions into a two-volume treatise of history, arithmetic and observation, followed by shorter analytic works on the nature, measure and laws of value, on rents and tithes, and on the deposits and currency. He wrote also a substantial article on Population for the Supplement to the Encyclopaedia Britannica, extended in 1836, and a work of moral philosophy, the Principles of Political Economy, whose first volume appeared in 1820. His manner is less technical than that of the economists who followed: he reasons on evidence drawn from travellers, parish registers and the history of nations, and he writes to persuade a cultivated reader as well as a specialist.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, measured and heavily qualified expository prose, built on the recurring couple of a check and a tendency, on numbered divisions and on the patient accumulation of instances; a polemical edge reserved for the openings and the conclusions of chapters. Abstract nouns and careful definitions are handled as instruments, and the argument advances by concession and exception rather than by system. Later economic writing becomes drier, more definitional and more preoccupied with measuring terms.
intellectual_concerns: The ratio of population to food and the geometric and arithmetic growth of the two; the moral and physical checks that keep the balance; the effects of parish relief and early marriage on the labouring poor; the reality of a general glut in contrast to Say's doctrine of markets; the theory of rent and the interests of landlords; the limits of perfectibility arguments and the uses of inequality; the education and moral discipline of the industrious classes.
historical_significance: The Essay on the Principle of Population set the terms on which famine, marriage, wages and relief were argued for a century, gave political economy its first professional professorship in England, and through Ricardo's debates defined the classical theory of rent. Its argument was taken up, and fought over, by poor-law reformers, by the reviewers of the Edinburgh and Quarterly, and by the evolutionary theorists who read in its competition for food the mechanism of natural selection; its pessimistic version of economics earned the science the name the dismal one. As a specimen of Romantic-period prose of argument he stands between the philosophical reformers of the 1790s and the professional social science of the 1830s.
biographical_uncertainty: The day of his birth is given variously as 13 or 14 February 1766 in the biographies, and the parish and estate are described both as Westcott and as the Rookery near Dorking. The anonymous first edition of 1798 was long attributed to others, and its precise relationship to the much enlarged second edition of 1803 is a matter of continuing scholarly description rather than of settled fact.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; Rationalist dissenting and radical philosophical prose of the 1790s
literary_identity: Dissenting minister turned philosopher, essayist and novelist; the systematic exponent of justice, private judgement and the indefinite perfectibility of the mind, and the era's most influential builder of a rational anarchism.
biography: Godwin was born at Wisbech in Cambridgeshire on 3 March 1756, the son of a Strict Baptist minister, and was intended for the dissenting ministry. He was trained at Hoxton Academy and served as an independent pastor at Ware and then at St Alphage's, Canary Street, in London, where he began to move from Calvinism towards Socinian and philosophical opinions. Publicly avowing deist and anti-monarchical views, he resigned his pulpit around 1783 and lived thereafter by his pen, befriending Samuel Holcroft, Thomas Holcroft and the circle of the radical book-seller and reform. An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice (1793) made his name overnight; his second edition, rewritten while the printers waited, already softened the strictest conclusions. In 1797 he married Mary Wollstonecraft, whose Rights of Men and Vindication of the Rights of Woman he had long admired and whose Memoirs of the Author of a Vindication of the Rights of Woman he published in 1798 to general disgust; their daughter Mary, later Mary Shelley, was born a few months before Wollstonecraft's death in childbed. The reopening of the Baker Street lecture rooms after the Gagging Acts, his campaign against the war with France, the essays of the Political Register and the Friend of the People, and the Enquiry's revised third edition of 1798 kept him at the centre of a shrinking radical public. His later career was long and increasingly domestic and literary: the novels and romances of the 1800s, the Life of Chatham, histories of England and of Commonwealth, a Life of Marat and the Essays; and the Courtauld lectures on necromancy. He was by then regarded as a venerable rather than a dangerous figure, died in London on 7 April 1836, and was buried beside Wollstonecraft in Bunhill Fields.
literary_profile: His work is a continuous prose project rather than a body of separate genres: a philosophical treatise on justice and government, a series of novels that test the same principles in the passions, and a large occaional literature of biography, history, political pamphlet and review essay. Enquiry Concerning Political Justice states the system in three parts on political justice, its application to government and punishment, and the morals and opinions that a rational institution would produce; the Dissertation on First Principles of Government of 1795 reissued the political portions as a shorter, more practical argument. Caleb Williams (1794) is at once a gothic narrative and an illustration of how institutional power and curiosity destroy an individual. His late prose turned to the history of ideas, to literature and to elaborate accounts of opinion, superstition and civilisation, in a manner closer to learned essay than to polemic.
stylistic_characteristics: A severe, unhurried argumentative prose of long balanced periods, abstract nouns and repeated key terms, in which a proposition is stated, qualified and restated until its consequences are exhausted; occasional polemic sharpened by irony and by plain contempt for argument from authority. In the novels and romances the same analytical habit appears as an insistence on motives, causes and the chain of reasoning that betrays a character, and the narrative voice is frequently intrusive and explanatory. Late work is digressive, bookish and cumulative rather than epigrammatic.
intellectual_concerns: Private judgement and the duty to follow the evidence of one's own reason; the opposition of justice to institution, and of general utility to promise, contract and allegiance; the critique of government, of coercion, of property held by inheritance and of marriage as an exclusive compact; the perfectibility of the mind and the gradual withering of political authority; the relation of opinion to virtue, and of literature and narrative to moral improvement; the morality of publication and the duty to tell truth.
historical_significance: Godwin supplied the first fully reasoned anarchism in English and gave radical thought of the 1790s its most systematic text; the Enquiry became a recognised authority for reformers, and its fame was such that it was read widely, answered in the press and cited in Parliament. He shaped, more than any single writer, the philosophical temper of the Romantic generation that grew up under the reputation of his principles, and his domestic history, as Wollstonecraft's husband and Mary Shelley's father, places him at the source of Frankenstein. His novels established the analytical, socially-caused English narrative; his Essays and histories kept the eighteenth-century argument about superstition, opinion and civilisation alive into the nineteenth century.
biographical_uncertainty: The chronology of his education at Hoxton Academy and the precise dating of his early pastorates at Ware and in Canary Street are variously given in the biographies; the full account of his marriage and of Wollstonecraft's death depends on his own Memoirs, published in 1798 and immediately contested by readers as injudicious.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the commercial, dissenting and abolitionist culture of Liverpool, and the Whig historical scholarship of the revolutionary decade
literary_identity: Merchant, banker, lawyer, historian of Renaissance Italy, abolitionist poet and patron of arts and botany; the first considerable English historian of the Medici and one of the earliest and most consistent English poet-critics of the slave trade.
biography: Roscoe was born at Liverpool on 8 March 1753, the only surviving son of a small trader in the market-garden and bowling-green line, and was educated at the dissenting and proprietary schools of the town before being bound apprentice to a Liverpool merchant house. Called upon to support a widowed mother and young sisters, he studied law, was admitted an attorney, and in the years of the town's enormous prosperity built up a mercantile and banking business of large reputation, at the same time pursuing scholarship, botany and the collection of pictures and books with a single-mindedness unusual in a tradesman. The Wrongs of Africa, a poem, published in two parts in 1787 and 1788 for the cause of the abolition committee, made him at once known beyond Liverpool and marked him permanently in his own town, where the slave-trade interest was powerful and where he was afterwards burnt in effigy. His two great historical works, the Life of Lorenzo de' Medici called the Magnificent of 1796, with its introductory view of Italian history, and the Life and Pontificate of Leo the Tenth of 1805, were built partly out of manuscripts which he obtained in Italy at his own cost, and gave the English reading public its first scholarly account of the age in which the revival of letters and the Reformation met. Elected in 1806 one of the first two members for the newly enfranchised town, he sat a single session, voting against the trade and against the party that had returned him, and withdrew from Parliament with his banking interests already embarrassed. The commercial crash of the post-war years ruined his firm about 1814-1815, and the sale of his library, his garden and his pictures, which included the sculptures and the collection of prints he had gathered with so much care, was a public event in the town. He gave his remaining years to letters, to botanical and artistic patronage and to the small poems and fables for children of which The Butterfly's Ball and the Grasshopper's Feast is the survivor, and he died at Liverpool on 27 June 1831, leaving a reputation as the scholar-tradesman of the great trading community and a family of sons, one of whom wrote his Life.
literary_profile: His work runs in three unrelated veins, all of them considerable. The abolitionist poem The Wrongs of Africa, in two parts, puts the whole progress of the trade, from the coast of Africa through the voyage to the colonies, into the heroic line of the moral plea. The Italian histories are scholarly narrative biography on the model of the eighteenth-century life, prefaced by disquisitions on the state of Italy and of the papacy and resting on printed authorities and on transcripts gathered in Italian libraries. The nursery verse, of which the insect masquerade is the most durable, belongs to the new small-book trade of the years after 1800, and he wrote also fables, translations from the Italian, botanical and historical essays, and the manuscripts on painting and on his own collection which his son printed after his death.
stylistic_characteristics: A decorous and deliberate eighteenth-century prose, grave in the histories, heavily qualified in the argumentative prefatory disquisitions, and circumstantial in the narrative of courts and councils; the abolition verse is in a stately heroic line of moral appeal, addressed to the conscience of a nation, with the enumeration of instances doing the rhetorical work. The nursery pieces are light, quick and plain, in short common metres of the child's ear, and show the same gift of concrete description that marks his botanical writing.
intellectual_concerns: The sin and the national interest of the slave trade, and the duty of a trading community to examine its own gains; the civilisation of Renaissance Italy, the papacy, and the fate of Italian liberty; the study of the age of the Medici as a case in the relation of letters, power and church; the encouragement of the fine arts and of botany in a commercial town; the instruction and the innocent fancy of very young children; the education and patronage of a manufacturing community.
historical_significance: The Wrongs of Africa was the first of the great abolition poems and gave the movement its earliest sustained verse indictment, published by the friends of the cause in the year of the first petition to Parliament; his Italian biographies founded the scholarly English study of the Renaissance and long stood as the standard accounts of Lorenzo and of Leo the Tenth. As a banker, collector and civic patron he made Liverpool a provincial centre of art and learning, and his ruin and the sale of his collections became the cautionary case of the merchant-scholar; his nursery poem passed into the childhood of two continents.
biographical_uncertainty: A few older biographical accounts place his birth in London rather than Liverpool, and the day of his death is given as the 27th or the 30th of June 1831. The extent of his responsibility for anonymous pamphlets on the trade and on the affairs of the town is not settled, and the account of his Italian manuscript researches depends largely on the prefaces to the two lives and on the family Life edited by his son, which is a defence as well as a record.
